en: Record of the Ordination of Bhikṣuṇīs, composed by the śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoxianglin Monastery in Nanhai, Guangzhou, while residing at Zaiqiu.

I humbly examine the origins and the historical development of how the precepts are received in both Central and Border regions. According to the regulations of the Middle Kingdom, one receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) before a group of ten; however, in the border regions, it is permitted for five persons.
One obtains the precepts. The Middle [Country] is Central India (Madhyadeśa). To the eastern border of India is the country of Pāṭaliputra;

to the southern border is the Śānti Stūpa; to the western border is the mountain of the Ṛṣi Ekaśaila; and to the northern border is the Pillar Kingdom (Yūpārāja). Beyond these four borders, they are called frontier countries.
China lies more than twenty-seven thousand *li* to the east of Pāṭaliputra. Five persons who maintain the Vinaya may perform the ordination ceremony there.
They received the full precepts (*mahā-upasampadā*). In the past, during the early reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, the two Dharma Masters Mātanga and Dharmaratna came to this land.
When they granted ordination to others, they merely shaved their hair and beards, had them don the *saṃkakṣikā* robe, and conferred upon them only the five and ten precepts.

Because one could not receive full ordination with fewer than five persons, for more than a hundred years until the reign of Emperor Huan of the Han dynasty, the three refuges, the five precepts, and the ten precepts were transmitted from one to another.
After Emperor Huan, five śramaṇas, including Zhi Falin, arrived in the land of Han from North India;
it was then that they began bestowing the full precepts upon others in Chang’an.

At that time, the Great Vinaya had not yet arrived; only the *Śīlaskandha* (Precepts Manual) in one fascicle and the *Karmavācanā* (Ritual Manual) in one fascicle were circulating in this land, transmitted through oral recitation.

When a community of nuns came seeking to receive the full ordination, the five monks said, "As clarified in the Vinaya, the full precepts may be conferred by a quorum of five monks only in frontier regions;
this does not apply to the community of nuns. At that time, the nuns withdrew and returned, weeping tears.

It was like rain falling. In the third year of the early Cao Wei period, Dharmakāla (translated as Fashí) from Central India arrived in Luoyang and translated the Vinaya, establishing the ritual procedures for ordination (*karmavācanā*) based on the requirement of ten monks. Thereupon, the Buddha-dharma spread extensively throughout China.

This was the beginning of the reception of the precepts and the Vinaya in the Eastern Land (China). During the end of the Han dynasty and the beginning of the Wei dynasty, two nuns from the kingdom of East India arrived in Chang’an.
Upon seeing the assembly of nuns there, they asked, "From whom did you receive the precepts?
The nuns replied, "We went to the Great Assembly (the monks) and received only the five precepts and the ten precepts. The two nuns sighed and said, "The nuns in this borderland..."
The assembly had not yet completed their full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). She immediately returned to her home country and converted fifteen people to come with her;

three died in the Snowy Mountains, two fell into a black ravine and perished, and only ten remained when they arrived here. All the nuns went to the capital, where she conferred the full precepts upon them.
Later, she traveled to the land of Wu and likewise conferred the full precepts upon the community of nuns there. The Western nuns then felt a deep longing for her.
Hōjō subsequently boarded a ship and returned to the South Seas. By the time he reached the vessel, there were only seven people remaining; three had lost their lives during the journey.

The entire trip, both going and returning, took more than ten years. Furthermore, according to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), in the tenth year of the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, the Indian monk Saṃghavarman arrived in Jiankang and was commanded by imperial decree to reside at Pinglu Temple for the sake of the capital’s śramaṇa Huizhao.
Three hundred and seventy people crossed to the shore of Caizhou and received the full precepts (*upasampadā*) once more on board the ship. Someone asked him for his reason, and Sengzhao replied:

"Because I doubted my previous reception—whether it was middling or inferior—I seek to further increase its excellence; therefore, I must receive them again. He maintained his original seniority in the monastic order.
In the eleventh year, Guṇavarman established a *sīmāmaṇḍala* at Nanlin Temple and conferred the precepts upon monks and nuns.
This was the beginning of the ordination platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) for the Land of China.
Not long after the eight bhikṣuṇīs from Siṃhala arrived, three more bhikṣuṇīs named Tiexuoluo (Tatsarā) came, completing the quorum of ten.

They then requested Saṃghavarman to serve as their preceptor, and for the sake of the bhikṣuṇī Huiguo and others of Jingfu Temple, they underwent the double ordination according to the two divisions of the Vinaya at the Southern Forest Ordination Platform.

He conferred the precepts upon more than three hundred people. Alas! The ancients forgot their own bodies for the sake of the Dharma and did not shrink from traveling tens of thousands of li to come here.
How can those who receive the precepts in this land not give rise to the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find? It is a pity that we now live in the age of the Final Dharma.

It is difficult to find those who understand the Dharma and can properly administer the *karmavācanā*. Furthermore, the transmission of the precepts for both the Bhikṣu and Bhikṣuṇī Saṃghas has long been lost.

In the past, even Mahinda the Arhat and other worthy sages—most of whom were saints established in the fruits of the path—dared not violate the Vinaya by bestowing full ordination upon others when the quorum of monks was incomplete, nor did they grant the Great Precepts to nuns with only a single division of the Saṃgha present. What kind of people are we, compared to them?

"To dare to contravene the Buddha’s teachings and extinguish the Buddha’s True Dharma would cause others to lose forever their status as bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, resulting in nothing more than a false name;
both the bestower and the recipient would thus commit an act that is contrary to the Dharma. In the fourteenth year of the Shunzhi era, I was in Yangcheng, Guangzhou.

At that time, nuns from various counties came seeking full ordination (*upasampadā*). Unable to decline their requests, I consequently established two groups of monks, each numbering ten, and conferred the great precepts upon them.
Thereafter, as it became difficult to find ten people, I would confer the ordination even when there were only five or more present, provided they were pure in their observance of the Vinaya.
Thus it is said: "In border regions, five who maintain the Vinaya may confer full ordination."

Regarding the precepts: the *upādhyāyī* (precept-giving teacher) must have completed ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*). As for the two teachers who perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) and the other witnesses, their years of seniority are not restricted;

however, they must necessarily be proficient in the Vinaya. Even if they have not yet mastered the Vinaya thoroughly, the one performing the *karmavācanā* must at least have a clear and precise understanding of the Vinaya before being permitted to preside over the ritual.
If it is not so, and one forcibly confers the precepts upon another, it will cause that person to [suffer].

If the precepts of long life do not moisten one's person, the transgression is no small matter. Although it is said that in frontier regions the five-member *saṃgha* may confer ordination, this does not include the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*).
This was because the ancients were cautious and reverent; even monks were difficult to find in frontier lands, so how could nuns be easily available?
From this, I infer that since the Vinaya permits monks [to be ordained], nuns must necessarily be included in the enumeration. Formerly, the Venerable Kātyāyana was in India...
In the country of Aparāntaka, there was the son of an elder named Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa who left the household life to seek the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

At that time, because there were not ten monks in that country, he was unable to receive the full ordination. He then went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha permitted that in border regions, five persons could confer the full ordination.

Since the circumstances of that time depended upon the *saṃgha*, the matter of nuns had not yet been discussed; how much more so now, in this age of the Final Dharma, when those who leave the household life encounter the True Teaching?
This is indeed difficult. If we do not take nuns into account, then the *bhikṣuṇī* order would be entirely deficient; who then would cultivate the Eight Respectful Observances?

Although this is a borderland, if there are ten pure individuals who uphold the Vinaya, one must specifically select five from among them. The Vinaya texts do not permit [arbitrary selection]; one must know that those who are not pure in their observance of the precepts are ineligible for selection.
Since the matter of receiving the precepts is of great significance, if even one person is not in accordance with the Dharma, the essence of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*) will be lost.
Nowadays, in various monastic assemblies, when bestowing full ordination upon others, they do not know how to perform the ritual for establishing the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*) of the Saṃgha;

if the boundary is not established, how can the ordination platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) be set up? Thus, the precepts cannot be obtained. Therefore it is said: "If the boundary is not established, all rituals such as *karmavācanā* and the reception of the precepts are performed in vain.
Furthermore, they do not perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) according to the Vinaya, relying instead solely on the teacher’s own mind while [the candidate] remains among the novices.

Standing before those clad in white robes, they fabricate their own doctrines and proclaim them; taking what is not Dharma to be Dharma, they transmit errors as errors, following one another in succession.

As this has persisted for a long time, they remain unaware of its fallacy. The Buddha said: "If there are those who uphold the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts, then the True Dharma has not yet perished from the world.
He further stated: "As long as the Vinaya-piṭaka remains, the Buddha-dharma also remains. Therefore, those who propagate and succeed [the teachings] must...

It is especially fitting to follow these instructions so that the True Dharma may endure forever and the *Prātimokṣa* may remain eternally firm. (The *Śīlakaṇḍa*, or ordination platform, is established within the Great Boundary.
The above is a brief account of the causes and conditions for obtaining the precepts.

Below, record the names of the Upādhyāya and Ācārya who conferred the precepts, as well as the names of the monks of the two assemblies, and note the year, month, day, and time of your own ordination, so as to distinguish the seniority and rank of one’s *śīla-varga*.

of [Lineage/Clan], a native of [District] County in [Prefecture],
received her teacher and left the household life on the [Day] of the [Month] of the [Year].
In the [Year] year, [Month] month, and [Day] day of the [Era Name], I received the śrāmaṇerī precepts from Upādhyāya [Name].
On the [Year] year, [Month] month, and [Day] day at [Time] hour, I received the [full ordination].

Appendix: Brief Ritual for the Procedure.
When a bhikṣuṇī first receives full ordination, she is not yet able to peruse the Mahāvinaya.

Her preceptor (upādhyāyī) and two teachers (ācāryas) should provide her with the Prātimokṣa-sūtra and cause her to read it thoroughly, so that she may know how to maintain it without committing any transgressions, and so that she may recognize the Poṣadha ceremony. From herself...
*Zi*: The methods for receiving robes, pure giving (*śuddhadāna*), and so forth.

Regarding the *poṣadha* method (the *poṣadha* held every half-month): even if there are as few as four bhikṣuṇīs present, they should recite the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. If fewer than four are present—namely three or two—they should perform the *poṣadha* face-to-face (*pratyekamukha*).
If there are any transgressions, one must first confess them before performing the *poṣadha*.

The Method for Reciting the Precepts Face-to-Face (On the day of the *poṣadha*, if there are three persons, each shall face the others, expose their heads, remove their sandals, and kneel with one knee on the ground, speaking as follows).
"Two elder sisters, attend with one-pointed mind. Today is the tenth day of the month for the Sangha to recite the precepts.
I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], am pure. (Recite this three times. The next two persons should likewise recite it. If there are only two persons, omit the first two characters and simply say, "Elder sister.")
The Method for Mindfully Reciting the Prātimokṣa (If there is only one person, one should recite it mentally and speak it aloud):
"Today is the [fifth] fourteenth day of the fortnight for the Saṃgha to recite the Prātimokṣa. I, the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, am pure. (Recite this three times.)
The Procedure for the Face-to-Face Retreat (Pūrvavārṣika; on the sixteenth day of the fourth month, one should address a bhikṣuṇī who knows the Dharma, saying):

"Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], shall dwell in reliance upon this certain monastery (*saṃghārāma*) [if it is within a village and not a place where the Saṃgha resides]."

One should say, "In such-and-such village" (or, if staying in a separate room, "in such-and-such room"). This is for the purpose of repairing dilapidated dwellings during the three-month summer retreat. (Recite this three times.)
He should say, "Very well. [The other] replies, "Excellent. (If it is the later retreat, when the sixteenth day of the fifth month arrives, one should say, "The latter three months.")
The Method for Mindful Residence during the Rains Retreat (If there is no person upon whom one relies, one performs the rite by speaking these words from one's own mind):
"I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], shall dwell in dependence upon a certain room in a certain location for the three-month summer rains retreat" (recite this three times).

The Procedure for Receiving Permission by Declaration (If there is business concerning the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, or an invitation from a donor, parents, or others, such that one cannot return on the same day— if two days are required, up to seven days—
one should speak to a bhikṣuṇī as follows).

"Venerable Sisters, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], having received the seven-day leave, shall go outside the boundary for the sake of a certain matter, and shall return here to observe the rains retreat.
I inform the Venerable Sisters so that they may know. (Recite this three times. One should not depart for the sake of food, drink, or clothing.
If the aforementioned matter cannot be completed within seven days, one should request from the Saṃgha a ten-day, half-month, or one-month leave through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).)

The Method of Self-Confession (Pravāraṇā) Face-to-Face: Whenever there is an offense, one should first confess it and only then perform the self-confession (*pravāraṇā*). If there are five bhikṣuṇīs residing at the monastery, they should appoint one among the Saṃgha to receive the self-confession on their behalf.
If there are not five, four should perform the face-to-face self-confession by facing one another and speaking as follows.
"Three elder sisters, please attend with one mind: today is the day of the *pravāraṇā* for the community of monks.
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], am pure regarding the *pravāraṇā*. (Recite this three times. If there are three or two persons, proceed in the same manner.)"
The Method for Mindful Invitation (Pravāraṇā) (If there is only one person, one should speak these words while reflecting in the mind):
"Today the Saṃgha performs the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*). I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], am pure regarding the invitation ceremony. (Recite three times.)

The Method for Receiving the Five Robes (The Buddha said: "The five robes should be formally received and maintained. If one possesses robes but does not maintain them, one incurs an offense. If they remain beyond ten days, one commits the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one obtains robes in accordance with the Dharma, one should assume a dignified demeanor and, before a bhikṣuṇī, or a preceptor (*upādhyāyī*), or a teacher (*ācāryā*), speak as follows):"

Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], receive this five-piece *antarvāsa* robe, consisting of one long and one short panel, as a cut-and-sewn garment (recite three times).

Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], receive this seven-strip uttarāsaṅga robe, consisting of two long pieces and one short piece, a cut-and-sewn garment (three times).
Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], am receiving this saṃghāṭī robe consisting of [number] strips, which has been [number] times patched.
[It is] long [by such-and-such a measure] and short [by such-and-such a measure].
I shall maintain this cut-and-sewn robe (three times). Sister, attend to me with one mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], receive this shoulder-covering robe;

it is four cubits in length and two and a half cubits in width. I shall maintain this shoulder-covering robe (three times. The Buddha ordained this because he feared the three robes might become soiled; one uses it to cover both shoulders before putting on the three robes over them).
"Venerable Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], accept this *kūṭāgāra* robe; it is four cubits long and two cubits wide.

This is the *kūṭāgāra* robe that I shall wear. (Recite this three times. *Kūṭāgāra* here means "basket-robe," which is the lower garment (*nivasana*). It is sewn together at both ends so that its shape resembles a small basket.

When wearing it, one tucks it inside and raises it above the navel, gathering both sides and pinning them double-layered against the spine, then fastening it with a cord. *Kūṭa* refers to a grain basket.)
The Ritual for Receiving the *niṣīdana* (Sitting Mat) (should be recited as follows):
"Venerable Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the Bhikṣuṇī [Name], am receiving this *niṣīdana* as my assistant robe.
(Recite three times.)
The Ritual for Receiving the Alms Bowl:
"Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], shall receive this pātra, which is of the proper measure, for the purpose of long-term use.
(Recite three times.)

The Method for Receiving Sixteen Utensils (one should receive the utensils on the very day they are obtained. If one requires them, sixteen may be kept; the remainder should be given as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*) or sent to others).
That is to say: a large cauldron, a small cauldron, two lids, a water jar with its lid, a rinsing vessel with its lid, four basins, two small ladles, and two large ladles (as received).
Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], this [item] is my sixteenth possession.
I now accept it. (Recite three times.)

Regarding the taking of medicine at improper times (the Buddha permitted the drinking of eight kinds of syrups, namely fruit juices such as those from pears, dates, sugarcane, grapes, lotus roots, and so forth; these should first be pressed by a pure person, filtered, and clarified.
One should receive them from the hand of a pure person and address a bhikṣuṇī, saying):
Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], because of the circumstance of a certain illness, have this [kind of] non-time beverage.
For the purpose of consuming it outside of the proper time, I now receive it from you, Sister. (Recite three times.)

Regarding the seven-day medicine (ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar): having received it once, one may take it with one's own hand and consume it for seven days. On the eighth day, one must give it away to others and may not consume it oneself. It should be stated as follows: [insert formula here].

Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], because of the circumstance of a certain illness, have this seven-day medicine for the purpose of consuming it while staying together for seven days. I now receive it from you, Sister (recite three times).

Medicines for life-long use (referring to pills, powders, and all salty or sour substances that are unfit to be eaten): having accepted them once, one may take and consume them oneself until they are exhausted. One should say: [formula].

Sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], because of the circumstance of a certain illness, shall receive from you, Sister, this medicine for life, in order to keep it overnight and take it regularly. (Recite three times.)

The Method for Purifying Gifts (There are two kinds of purification through giving: first, genuine giving; second, indirect purification through giving. Regarding genuine purification through giving, one should say as follows).
Sister, please attend to me with a single mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], possess this extra robe which has not yet been purified.

Now, for the sake of purification, I relinquish it to you, Sister, as a true purification (meaning a true relinquishment to another; if one wishes to wear it, one should ask the other and then wear it).

The Method for Successive Purification of Gifts (*Nettippādana-dharmma*). (Once a bhikṣuṇī has received the precepts, she must purify all her robes—both new and old—with the exception of the five [standard] robes—before one other bhikṣuṇī.

If she does not so declare them, after ten days she commits an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). Furthermore, regarding any robes subsequently acquired, whether they be cotton cloth or otherwise, even down to those measuring one chi and four cun in length and seven cun in width, she must immediately purify them by speaking as follows:)
"Venerable sister, please attend to me with one-pointed mind. I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have an extra robe that has not yet been purified.

For the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable sister, so that it may be purified through transfer. (The recipient of the purification should say: 'Venerable sister, you have this extra robe which has not yet been purified.
For the sake of purification, you give it to me; I now accept it. (Having accepted it, she says: 'To whom do you give it? (She replies: 'I give it to [Name].'"
[Name]. (The recipient of the purification says: "Sister, you possess this long robe which has not yet been purified. For the sake of purifying it, you give it to me;
I now accept it. Having accepted it, you give it to [Name]. This robe already belongs to [Name];

you must properly guard and wear it for [Name] according to the circumstances. (One should call upon the name of a specific bhikṣuṇī as the "purifier"—either the preceptor, the instructor, or another—and if that purifier dies, one must immediately designate another purifier. Taking...
Regarding all clothing and items previously possessed, one should perform the ritual of *śuddhika* (purification) by calling out the name of the subsequent pure owner.

All other procedures for performing rituals and maintaining dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) are fully detailed in the *Karmavācanā-mūla* (the root text of ritual actions) and within the *Daily Life of a Śramaṇa*; one should consult these sources accordingly.

The Eight Rules Not to Be Transgressed (also known as the Eight Rules of Respect). The Buddha said to Ānanda: "I now establish for women eight rules that must be observed for as long as life lasts and not transgressed.
If they can practice them, this constitutes receiving the precepts. What are these eight?"
First: Although she may be a bhikṣuṇī of a hundred years' standing, upon seeing a newly ordained bhikṣu, she should rise to meet him, pay homage, and arrange a clean seat for him to sit upon.
This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; it must not be transgressed as long as one lives.
2. A bhikṣuṇī must not revile or scold a bhikṣu, nor should she slander him by saying that he has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his deportment.
This rule should be respected (the rest of the wording is as stated above).
3. A bhikṣuṇī should not perform an *udghāta* (formal accusation) against a bhikṣu; she should not perform an *anusmṛti* (reminding);
she should not perform an *adhi-vacana* (self-accusation). She should not obstruct another’s search for an offense, nor obstruct the *poṣadha*, nor obstruct the *pravāraṇā*.
A bhikṣuṇī should not reprove a bhikṣu; a bhikṣu should reprove a bhikṣuṇī. Such is the rule, which should be respected (*the remainder as above*).
4. Once the śikṣamāṇā has completed her training in the precepts, she shall request the full ordination from the community of bhikṣus. This is the proper procedure:
[she] should show respect... (the remainder of the formula is as above).
5. When a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she should undergo the mānatva penance before both assemblies of the Saṃgha.
This rule should be respected (*the remainder of the wording is as above*).
6. A bhikṣuṇī should, every half-month, request instruction from the saṃgha. This rule should be respected (the rest as above).
7. A bhikṣuṇī should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) where there are no bhikṣus.
This rule should be respected (the rest as above).
8. When the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has completed the summer retreat (varṣā), they should request the three matters of *pravāraṇā* (self-criticism) from within the Bhikṣu Saṃgha:
what has been seen, heard, or suspected. This rule should be respected [as the remaining wording is as above]. Thus, Ānanda, I now declare these eight rules that must not be transgressed.
It is as if a person were to build a bridge over a great body of water to cross it; if a woman can...
The Practitioner. This refers to the reception of the precepts (and so forth).
The Record of the Reception of Precepts for Bhikṣuṇīs (concludes).
